title_ar: الكلام على شرح ابن أبي العز للعقيدة الطحاوية
title_en: On Ibn Abi al-Izz's Commentary on the Tahawi Creed
body_ar:
ما صحة كتاب ابن أبي العز في شرحه على عقيدة الطحاوي وهل فيه أخطاء وما هي إذا كانت موجودة؟

أن البويطي ذكر عن الشافعي رحمه الله قال: لما أكمل الشافعي كتابه ناولنيه فقال: خذ هذا الكتاب على خطإ كثير فيه، قال: قلت يا أبا عبد الله أصلحه لنا، قال: كيف وقد قال الله تعالى: {وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِنْدِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا} أبى الله العصمة إلا لكتابه،

فمن لا ينتفع بكتاب فيه خطأ فعليه أن يلزم القرآن وحده وأن يرد كل ما سواه من الكتب، القرآن وحده هو الذي لا خطأ فيه، أما ما سواه من الكتب فلا بد أن تبقى فيها الأخطاء وذلك من عصمة الله للقرآن وحفظه،

وعموما فهذا الكتاب الذي اشتهر بشرح ابن أبي العز على عقيدة الطحاوي هو شرح وجد لهذه العقيدة ولم يذكر مؤلفه ولم يسم لكن عرف في ترجمة ابن أبي العز الحنفي أنه من شراح هذه العقيدة وشراحها كثر ومؤلفها قديم عاصر أصحاب الكتب الستة وعاش في حياة الإمام أحمد، وهو تلميذ للمزني وابن أخته، المزني صاحب الشافعي ووارثه في العلم، والطحاوي هو أحمد بن جعفر بن سلامة الطحاوي تلميذ المزني وابن أخته،

وقد كان في بداية شبابه شافعيا ثم انتقل إلى المذهب الحنفي، وسبب ذلك أنه أراد خاله أن يعلمه مختصره في الفقه وهو المختصر الذي اختصر به الأم للشافعي فتشاغل عنه في مصر، فقال: والله لا يطلع منك خير، أي لا تأتي بخير، وقسمه إنما هو مبني على بساط يمينه وهو ما عرف من عدم جد هذا الطالب في الطلب، فغضب الطالب من هذه الكلمة فخرج في طلب العلم حتى بَرَّزَ فيه، فلما ألف كتابه المختصر في فقه الحنفية قال: رحم الله خالي لو رأى كتابي هذا لكفر عن يمينه،

وعموما فإن الإمام الطحاوي رحمه الله من الذين نفع الله بعلمهم فيما بعد، وكتبه نافعة كثيرة منها مشكل الآثار الذي هو من أجل الأسفار في هذا الباب، ومنها شرح معاني الآثار وهو من مراجع الحديث المعتمدة، ومنها مختصره في المذهب الحنفي، ومنها عقيدته المشهورة بالطحاوية وغير ذلك من كتبه المعروفة،

وهذا الشرح هو مثل غيره من الشروح تضمن علما جما وخيرا كثيرا، وفيه كثير من الأحاديث الصحيحة والآثار الصحيحة عن السلف، وفيه شرح وبيان لما ذكره الطحاوي رحمه الله مختصرا من عقيدة أبي حنيفة وأبي يوسف ومحمد بن الحسن الشيباني في عقيدته، فهو من الكتب التي ينتفع بها طلاب العلم

ولا بد أن يعلموا أن كل كتاب فيه الخطأ والصواب، فلو اطلع الإنسان على خطإ فيه فليس له أن يشهر به وأن يجعل من الحبة قبة، فهذا ليس من هدي طلاب العلم ولا هو من سلوك أهل العلم، بل قد قال ابن القيم رحمه الله: «زلات العلماء أقذار وهم بحار وإذا بلغ الماء قلتين لم يحمل الخبث».
body_en:
What is the standing of Ibn Abi al-Izz's book, his commentary on the creed of al-Tahawi? Does it contain errors, and what are they if there are any?

Al-Buwayti related from al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him. He said: when al-Shafi'i had finished his book he handed it to me and said: 'Take this book, with much error in it.' He said: I said, 'Abu Abd Allah, put it right for us.' He said: 'How, when God, exalted, has said: {And had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:82)? God has refused to grant preservation from error to anything but His own Book.'

So whoever cannot benefit from a book that contains an error must hold to the Qur'an alone and reject every book besides it. The Qur'an alone is what has no error in it; as for the books besides it, errors must remain in them, and that is part of God's preserving and safeguarding of the Qur'an.

In general, this book, well known as Ibn Abi al-Izz's commentary on the creed of al-Tahawi, is a commentary on this creed that was found, its author neither stated nor named; but it was established, in the biographical notice of Ibn Abi al-Izz al-Hanafi, that he is one of the commentators on this creed — and its commentators are many. Its author is of early date: he was a contemporary of the authors of the six books and lived in the lifetime of Imam Ahmad; and he was a student of al-Muzani and his sister's son — al-Muzani being al-Shafi'i's companion and his heir in knowledge. Al-Tahawi is Ahmad ibn Jafar ibn Salamah al-Tahawi, the student of al-Muzani and his sister's son.

At the beginning of his youth he was a Shafi'i, and then he moved to the Hanafi school. The reason for that is that his maternal uncle wanted to teach him his own abridgement in fiqh — the abridgement by which he abridged al-Shafi'i's al-Umm — and he let himself be distracted from it in Egypt. So the uncle said: 'By God, no good will come out of you' — that is, you will bring forth nothing good. His oath rested only on the ground on which it was sworn, namely what he had observed of this student's lack of seriousness in seeking knowledge. The student was angered by these words and went out in pursuit of knowledge until he became pre-eminent in it. Then, when he composed his book the Abridgement, in Hanafi fiqh, he said: 'May God have mercy on my uncle; had he seen this book of mine he would have made expiation (kaffārah) for his oath.'

In general, Imam al-Tahawi, may God have mercy on him, is among those by whose knowledge God brought benefit afterwards. His beneficial books are many: among them Mushkil al-Āthār, which is one of the most eminent volumes in this field; among them Sharḥ Maʿānī al-Āthār, which is one of the relied-upon references in hadith; among them his abridgement in the Hanafi school; among them his creed, famous as al-Ṭaḥāwiyyah; and other well-known books of his.

This commentary is like other commentaries: it contains abundant knowledge and much good. In it are many sound hadiths and sound reports from the salaf, and in it is commentary and clarification of what al-Tahawi, may God have mercy on him, set down in brief in his creed, of the creed of Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani. It is among the books from which students of knowledge derive benefit.

They must know that every book contains both error and what is correct. So if a person comes upon an error in it, it is not for him to publicise it and to make a dome out of a grain. That is not of the guidance of students of knowledge, nor is it of the conduct of the people of knowledge. Rather, Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, said: 'The slips of the scholars are filth, but they themselves are oceans; and when water reaches two qullahs, it does not carry impurity.'

flags.arabic: وهل فيه أخطاء وما هي إذا كانت موجودة؟
flags.context: the second half of the question, which the Sheikh does not answer
options: render the question in full and leave it unanswered, as the source does
display with a note that the specific errors are not identified in the written text
withhold until the Sheikh's office supplies the missing part
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. The questioner asks what the errors in the commentary are. The Sheikh answers that every book but the Qur'an contains error, praises the commentary, and counsels against publicising a scholar's slips — but he never names a single error in it. A reader who is not warned will take 'in it are many sound hadiths and sound reports' as a clean bill of health, which is not what he says. Nothing has been supplied.

flags.arabic: والطحاوي هو أحمد بن جعفر بن سلامة الطحاوي
flags.context: والطحاوي هو أحمد بن جعفر بن سلامة الطحاوي تلميذ المزني وابن أخته
options: translate the name exactly as the source gives it and flag
translate as given with a bracketed note of the usual form of the name
give the name in the form standard in the biographical literature
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT, not corrected. The name is given here as Ahmad ibn Jafar ibn Salamah; the biographical literature gives al-Tahawi as Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Azdi al-Tahawi. Per style guide §11 the source has been translated as it stands and the discrepancy recorded rather than silently repaired.

flags.arabic: ومؤلفها قديم عاصر أصحاب الكتب الستة وعاش في حياة الإمام أحمد
options: translate exactly as given and flag the dating
translate as given with a bracketed note on the dates
adjust the statement to the conventional dates
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT, not corrected. Al-Tahawi is conventionally dated 239–321 AH, and Imam Ahmad died in 241 AH, so 'lived in the lifetime of Imam Ahmad' can only be true of al-Tahawi's infancy. This is the kind of slip that occurs in a spoken answer; it has been translated exactly and recorded here rather than repaired.

flags.arabic: وقسمه إنما هو مبني على بساط يمينه
flags.context: فقال: والله لا يطلع منك خير، أي لا تأتي بخير، وقسمه إنما هو مبني على بساط يمينه وهو ما عرف من عدم جد هذا الطالب في الطلب
options: his oath rested only on the ground on which it was sworn
his oath was made only in the light of the circumstances that prompted it
his oath was governed by the context of his swearing
flags.note: بساط اليمين is a technical expression in the law of oaths: the circumstance or occasion in view of which an oath is sworn, which limits how the oath is construed. The Sheikh uses it to explain why the uncle's oath was not a judgement on the student's whole future — and this is what makes the closing remark about expiation intelligible. All three renderings are readable; the first keeps closest to the Arabic image.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The report from al-Buwayti shifts between third-person narration and al-Buwayti's own first person mid-sentence, exactly as the source has it. The shift has been kept rather than smoothed out.
The Sheikh gives no grading for the report from al-Buwayti or for the saying of Ibn al-Qayyim, and none has been supplied.
'To make a dome out of a grain' (أن يجعل من الحبة قبة) is the Arabic idiom for making a mountain out of a molehill; the Arabic image has been kept because the Sheikh's next sentence builds on it.

Ibn al-Qayyim's saying turns on the ruling that a quantity of water reaching two qullahs is not rendered impure by contact with impurity. The wordplay between the scholars as 'oceans' and that ruling is in the Arabic and has been kept.
